pages.title: Landlord Reference Letter
pages.description: A landlord reference letter is a current or former landlord's signed statement about one tenancy: the address, the dates, the rent, the payment record, and whether they would rent to you again. Build one in the browser below, from either side of the request.
pages.summary: Ask a landlord for facts they can check against their own ledger — dates, rent, late count, notice history — instead of praise. A checkable letter survives a screening review; a warm one gets skimmed and set aside.
pages.definition: A landlord reference letter is a signed statement from a current or former landlord describing one specific tenancy: the rental address, the dates the tenant lived there, the rent amount, the payment record, and whether the landlord would rent to that tenant again.
pages.definitionDetail: It is written in prose and it carries an opinion, which is what separates it from a rental verification form (a fixed field sheet with no opinion) and from a tenant screening report (a consumer report bought by the landlord from a screening company, which the tenant does not write and cannot edit).

keyFacts: The letter belongs to the landlord, not the tenant. A tenant can draft a version and ask the landlord to confirm and sign it, but a leasing office treats a letter the tenant signed themselves as a self-statement, not a reference.

Corporate property managers frequently have a written policy that limits them to confirming dates, rent, and balance. That is not a refusal; ask for the facts-only version rather than pressing for an opinion they are not allowed to give.
The reference is checked. A leasing agent who has any doubt calls the number on the letter, so the phone number and email must be the landlord's real business contact, not a friend standing in.

The Fair Housing Act applies to what a landlord writes as much as to who they rent to. A reference that comments on a tenant's family size, disability, national origin, or religion creates a fair-housing problem for the landlord who wrote it.
A reference letter does not replace proof of income or a credit check. It answers one question — how this person rented — and leaves the other questions to other documents.

Tenancy start date and end date, or a statement that the tenancy is current

steps: Ask the leasing office what they will accept: a signed letter, a completed verification form, or a phone call. Some accept only one, and building the wrong one costs you a week.
Ask your landlord early, and ask in writing. A landlord who is asked by text on a Friday afternoon writes a worse letter than one who gets a written request with the facts already listed.
Send the landlord the facts you already know — address, dates, rent — so they are confirming a record rather than reconstructing one from memory.
Let the landlord write the opinion sentence in their own words. A letter where every sentence sounds like the tenant wrote it reads as coached.
Check every date and amount against your lease and your payment records before the letter goes out. A rent figure that is $50 off is the kind of thing a screener notices.
Ask for it on letterhead or from the landlord's business email address, and keep a copy of what was sent and when.
reviewChecklist: Every date matches the lease, not your memory of it.
The rent figure matches what you actually paid, including any mid-tenancy increase.
The landlord's phone number and email are ones that will be answered during business hours.
Nothing in the letter mentions family, health, disability, religion, or national origin.
The letter names one tenancy and one address, not a general character reference.

pages.templateTitle: Short reference, for a landlord who wants three sentences
pages.template:
[Landlord letterhead] — [Date]

To the leasing office,

[Tenant name] rented [full address] from [start date] to [end date] at [monthly rent] per month. [Tenant name] paid rent in full and on time, no notices were served during the tenancy, and the unit was returned in good condition with the deposit refunded in full.

I would rent to [tenant name] again. I can be reached at [business phone] or [business email] to confirm any of this.

[Landlord name], [title]
pages.alternateTitle: Reference where the payment record is not clean
pages.alternateTemplate:
[Landlord letterhead] — [Date]

To the leasing office,

[Tenant name] rented [full address] from [start date] to [end date] at [monthly rent] per month.

[Tenant name] was late on rent [number] times, in [month/year] and [month/year]. In each case the balance was paid in full within [number] days and no eviction was filed. The remainder of the tenancy was paid on time, and the unit was returned in good condition.

On that record, I would rent to [tenant name] again.

[Landlord name], [title], [business phone], [business email]
mistakes: Writing the letter yourself and asking the landlord only to sign it. Leasing agents read a lot of these and a tenant-voiced letter is obvious; ask the landlord to put the opinion sentence in their own words.

Using a friend, a relative, or a personal cell number in place of the real landlord. The reference gets called, and a reference that does not check out is worse for the application than no reference at all.
Asking for praise instead of facts. A letter that says a tenant was wonderful and gives no dates, no rent figure, and no payment record settles nothing a screener needs settled.
Hiding a late payment the ledger will show anyway. A reference that says the record was spotless next to a screening report showing two late months damages everything else in the packet.
Letting the landlord mention children, a medical situation, an immigration status, or a religion. It does not help the tenant and it exposes the landlord to a fair-housing complaint.

faq.question: What should a landlord reference letter include?
faq.answer: The rental address, the tenancy dates, the monthly rent, the payment record, any notices served, the condition of the unit at move-out, a direct answer on whether the landlord would rent to the tenant again, and the landlord's business contact so the reference can be verified.

faq.question: Can I write my own landlord reference letter?
faq.answer: You can draft it and send it to your landlord to correct and sign, and doing so usually gets you a faster reply. What you cannot do is sign it yourself and submit it as a reference — a leasing office treats that as your own statement, which is a different and much weaker thing.

faq.question: What if my old landlord will not write one?
faq.answer: Ask instead for the facts-only confirmation, which many management companies are permitted to send when a full reference is not. If that is also refused, substitute the evidence you control: cancelled rent cheques, bank statements showing the transfers, the signed lease, and the return of your deposit.

faq.question: Is a landlord reference letter the same as rental verification?
faq.answer: No. A reference letter is written prose with an opinion in it. A rental verification form is a fixed set of fields the landlord completes with no opinion, usually on a form the new landlord or housing agency supplies. Some applications ask for one, some for the other, and a few for both.

faq.question: How long should it be?
faq.answer: One page, and usually three or four sentences. A leasing agent reading dozens of applications gives it perhaps twenty seconds, so the dates, the rent, and the payment record should all be visible without scrolling.

faq.question: Does a strong reference letter guarantee I get the apartment?
faq.answer: No. It settles one question among several. Income, credit, occupancy limits, pets, and the timing of other applications all sit outside what any reference letter can influence.

pages.title: Rental Verification Form
pages.description: A rental verification form is the fixed field sheet a new landlord or housing agency sends to a previous landlord: dates, rent, balance owed, late count, notices, would-rent-again. Complete one below — with the tenant authorization that is the reason most of them come back blank.
pages.summary: Send the authorization with the form, not after it. A previous landlord who receives a verification request without written tenant consent is usually instructed to ignore it, which is why these forms sit unanswered for weeks.
pages.definition: A rental verification form is a structured request sent to a current or former landlord asking them to confirm one tenancy in checkable fields rather than in prose: the dates, the rent amount, any balance owed, the number of late payments, the notices served, and whether they would rent to the tenant again.
pages.definitionDetail: It is filled in by the landlord and returned to whoever sent it — a leasing office, a mortgage underwriter documenting rent history, or a public housing agency. Unlike a reference letter it contains no opinion beyond the final question, and unlike a screening report it comes from the landlord's own records rather than from a consumer reporting agency.

keyFacts: Most previous landlords will not answer without written authorization from the tenant. A management company's standing instruction is to ignore an unsigned request, so the authorization is not a formality — it is the thing that makes the form answerable.

The form is returned to the requester, not to the tenant. A tenant who fills one in and hands it to the leasing office has produced a self-statement; the form only carries weight when it travels from the previous landlord's office directly to the requester.
Answers must come from the ledger, not from memory. A landlord who writes 'never late' and later produces a ledger showing two late months has created a contradiction that damages the tenant.

A verification form is a consumer inquiry in some contexts and not in others. When a landlord orders a screening report the Fair Credit Reporting Act applies; a direct landlord-to-landlord verification is not a consumer report, which is why it can be answered without a screening company.

There is no single national form. HUD supplies its own for voucher tenancies, mortgage underwriters use their own for rent history, and most leasing offices use one written in-house — so ask which one before you send anything.
fields: Tenant's full legal name and any co-tenant named on the lease
Full rental address including unit number
Previous landlord or management company name, phone, and email or fax
Requester's name, organization, and where the completed form should be returned
Lease start date and lease end date, or current-tenancy status
Monthly rent, and whether rent was ever increased during the tenancy
Any outstanding balance, and any amount charged against the deposit
Number of late payments, notices served, and whether an eviction was ever filed
The tenant's signed and dated authorization to release the rental history
steps: Ask the requester which form they want. If they have their own, use theirs; a substitute form is a common reason a file is returned as incomplete.
Have the tenant sign the authorization first. Send it in the same message as the form, not as a follow-up after the landlord has already ignored the request.
Address the request to the management office, not to an individual leasing agent who may have moved on. Include the property address in the subject line so it can be found by unit.
Give the landlord a deadline and a return path. A form with no return-by date and no fax or email goes to the bottom of the pile.
Ask the landlord to answer from the ledger. Anything they cannot support from their records should be left blank rather than guessed.
Follow up once by phone after 5 days. The most common outcome is not refusal, it is that the email went to a shared inbox nobody reads.
reviewChecklist: The tenant's authorization is signed and dated, and names the same address as the form.
The rental address on the form matches the lease exactly, unit number included.
There is a return-by date and a working return address, fax, or email on the form.
Every field the landlord answered can be supported from the rent ledger.
The form went from the previous landlord to the requester, not by way of the tenant.

Subject: Rental verification request — {{propertyAddress}} — {{tenantName}}

To the records office at {{landlordName}},

{{requesterName}} is processing a rental application from {{tenantName}}, who lists {{propertyAddress}} as a previous address. We are requesting verification of that tenancy.

The tenant's signed authorization to release this information is included with this request.

We are asking you to confirm, from your records:

  1. Lease start and end dates
  2. Monthly rent, and any increase during the tenancy
  3. Any balance currently outstanding
  4. The number of late payments
  5. Any notices served, including any eviction filing
  6. The security deposit outcome
  7. Whether your office would rent to this tenant again

Please leave blank anything your records do not support rather than estimating it.

Please return the completed form to {{returnTo}}{{#returnBy}} by {{returnBy}}{{/returnBy}}. If a different office handles verifications, we would be grateful if you could forward this on and let us know where it went.

Thank you,
{{requesterName}}
{{returnTo}}

mistakes: Sending the form without the tenant's signed authorization. This is the single largest cause of an unanswered verification, and it is fully preventable.
Letting the tenant carry the form. A verification that passes through the applicant's hands loses most of its value; it has to travel from the previous landlord's office to the requester.
Using your own form when the requester supplied one. Housing agencies and underwriters often cannot accept a substitute, and the file is returned as incomplete.
Answering fields from memory. A landlord who guesses at a late count and is later contradicted by their own ledger has damaged the tenant they were trying to help.
Sending it with no deadline and no return path. A request that does not say where to send the answer or by when is the easiest thing in a records inbox to defer.

faq.question: What is a rental verification form?
faq.answer: A fixed-field request sent to a current or former landlord asking them to confirm one tenancy from their own records: the dates, the rent, any balance owed, the number of late payments, the notices served, the deposit outcome, and whether they would rent to that tenant again.

faq.question: Who fills out a rental verification form?
faq.answer: The previous landlord or their management company. The requester — a leasing office, a mortgage underwriter, or a housing agency — sends it; the tenant signs the authorization that permits it to be answered; the landlord completes and returns it.

faq.question: Why do rental verification forms come back blank?
faq.answer: Most often because no signed tenant authorization was included, and a management company's standing instruction is to ignore unsigned requests. The next most common reasons are that it went to an individual agent who has left, or that it arrived with no return-by date and no return address.

faq.question: Can a tenant fill out their own rental verification form?
faq.answer: A tenant can pre-fill the tenancy details to save the landlord a lookup, and should sign the authorization. What a tenant cannot do is complete and return the form as though it came from the landlord — the value of the document is that it comes from the landlord's records.

faq.question: How long does rental verification take?
faq.answer: A small landlord often replies in 1 to 3 days. A management company's records office typically takes 5 to 10 days, and a first follow-up call after 5 days is usually what moves it.

faq.question: Is a verification form the same as a credit or screening check?
faq.answer: No. A verification form comes directly from the landlord's own tenancy records. A tenant screening report is a consumer report bought from a screening company and is governed by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, including the notice a landlord owes you if it is used against your application.

pages.description: An employment verification form is a fixed field sheet an employer completes and returns directly to whoever asked for it. Which form you need is decided by the requester, not by you — a mortgage file, a VA file, and a benefits office each require their own and none accepts a substitute.
pages.summary: Ask the requester which form they use before filling in anything. Mortgage underwriting uses Fannie Mae Form 1005, a VA loan file uses VA Form 26-8497, a state benefits office has its own, and Form I-9 is not a verification of employment at all.
pages.definition: An employment verification form is a structured request that an employer or payroll department completes on an employee's behalf — confirming employment dates, job title, current status, and, where written authorization exists, hours and compensation — and returns directly to the party that asked for it.
pages.definitionDetail: Two things separate it from the other documents it gets confused with. It is completed by the employer rather than the employee, and it travels from the employer to the requester without passing through the applicant's hands. A verification letter is prose the employer writes; Form I-9 is the employer's own work-authorization record and never leaves their files.

keyFacts: There is no single national employment verification form. Mortgage underwriting uses Fannie Mae Form 1005 or Freddie Mac Form 90, VA loan files use VA Form 26-8497, and most state benefits offices publish their own. Substituting one for another gets a file returned as incomplete.

Form I-9 is not an employment verification form. It records that an employer checked a new hire's identity and work authorization, it is kept in the employer's own files, and it is not sent to landlords, lenders, or agencies.
Written employee consent is normally required before payroll releases income. Employers that will confirm dates and title on a phone call will often not release pay without a signed release on file.

Many mid-size and large employers outsource verification entirely to an automated service. When they do, a form sent to HR will not be answered at all — the requester has to go through the service, and the employee may need to release a PIN or access code.
A form that reaches the requester by way of the applicant loses most of its value. Underwriters and caseworkers treat a verification the applicant handled as an applicant statement.
fields: Employee's full legal name and, where the form asks, the last four digits of the Social Security number
Employer's legal name, worksite address, and the payroll or HR contact who is authorized to verify
Job title and whether the position is full-time, part-time, seasonal, or contract
Date of hire, and the separation date where employment has ended
Current employment status as of the date the form is signed
Base pay rate, pay frequency, and average hours per week — only where the form asks and consent is on file
Overtime, bonus, or commission history where the form requests it, usually over the last 2 years
Verifier's name, title, direct phone, business email, signature, and date
The employee's signed authorization to release employment and income information
steps: Ask the requester which form they use and whether they will accept an alternative. Underwriters and benefits caseworkers usually cannot; landlords and new employers usually can.
Ask your employer how verification is handled before you send anything. If it is outsourced to an automated service, a form emailed to HR will sit unanswered and you will lose a week finding out.
Sign the release first. Send the authorization together with the form, not after payroll has already declined to answer.
Give payroll a return path and a deadline. Name the fax number, secure portal, or email the completed form goes to, and the date it is needed by.
Check the completed form against your own records before it goes out — hire date, title, pay rate, and pay frequency all have to match your pay stubs.
Follow up by phone after 5 business days. The usual cause of a stalled verification is a shared inbox nobody reads, not a refusal.
reviewChecklist: The form is the one the requester named, not a similar form from another program.
Your signed authorization is attached and dates from within the window the requester allows.
Every figure matches your most recent pay stubs, including pay frequency.
The verifier's phone number reaches a person who can confirm what they signed.
The completed form went from the employer to the requester, not through you.

Subject: Employment verification request — {{employeeName}}

Hello {{verifierName}},

{{requesterName}} has asked for verification of my employment with {{employerName}} in connection with {{purpose}}. My signed authorization to release this information is attached.

mistakes: Filling in the form yourself and having your manager sign it. Underwriters and caseworkers are trained to spot an applicant-completed form, and a wrong pay frequency in your own handwriting is worse than a delay.
Sending a benefits agency's form to a mortgage underwriter, or the reverse. The forms look similar and ask overlapping questions, and neither office will accept the other's.
Confusing Form I-9 with a verification of employment. Asking HR for a copy of your I-9 to send to a landlord will get a refusal and a delay.
Omitting the signed release, then reading payroll's refusal to disclose pay as an unwillingness to help.
Hand-carrying the completed form to the requester. A verification that passed through the applicant is treated as an applicant statement, which is not what was asked for.

faq.question: What is an employment verification form?
faq.answer: A structured request that an employer or payroll department completes, confirming employment dates, job title, current status, and — where a signed release exists — hours and pay, returned directly to the party that asked for it rather than to the employee.

faq.question: Which employment verification form do I need?
faq.answer: Whichever one the requester names. A conventional mortgage file uses Fannie Mae Form 1005 or Freddie Mac Form 90, a VA loan file uses VA Form 26-8497, state benefits offices publish their own, and landlords and new employers usually accept anything reasonable. Ask before you send anything.

faq.question: Can I fill out my own employment verification form?
faq.answer: You can pre-fill the factual details to save payroll a lookup, and you should sign the release. What you cannot do is complete it as though it came from the employer — the value of the document is that it comes from payroll records and travels directly to the requester.

faq.question: How long does an employment verification take?
faq.answer: A small employer often replies in 1 to 3 days. A large payroll department typically takes 5 to 10 days, and an automated verification service can answer the same day once the requester has the employer code. A follow-up call after 5 business days is usually what moves a stalled request.

faq.question: Is Form I-9 an employment verification form?
faq.answer: No. Form I-9 records that the employer examined a new hire's identity and work authorization documents. It is retained in the employer's files and is not the document a landlord, lender, or agency is asking for.

faq.question: What if my employer refuses to complete a form?
faq.answer: Many employers have a policy of confirming only dates, title, and status, and of routing anything further to a verification service. Ask which service and pass that on to the requester. Where nothing is available, substitute what you control: recent pay stubs, your W-2, and an IRS wage and income transcript.

atoms.title: field set

pages.definition: An employment verification letter is a short statement signed by an employer confirming that a named person works or worked at a named employer, giving the job title, the dates of employment, the current status, and — only where the employer is authorized to disclose it — the compensation.
pages.definitionDetail: It is prose rather than a form, which is what makes it flexible and what makes it weaker. keyFacts: The letter belongs to the employer. HR, payroll, or a manager with signing authority writes and signs it; a letter an employee wrote about themselves is a self-statement and gets read as one.

Include compensation only where the reader needs it and the employer is authorized to disclose it. A landlord usually needs income; a new employer usually does not; and putting salary in a letter that did not ask for it is the most common overshare on this document.
Every letter gets a phone call if anything about it is unusual. The verifier's direct line and business email carry more weight than the letterhead does.

Reason for separation does not belong in a verification letter. Many employers have a written policy against stating it, and volunteering it creates exposure for the employer and rarely helps the employee.
For a self-employed applicant there is no employer to sign. The equivalent is a client or contracting party confirming the engagement, alongside a CPA letter and the tax records that support it.

mistakes: Using one all-purpose template for every reader. A letter that includes salary, hours, duties, and separation history satisfies no reader well and overshares for four of the six.
Opening 'to whom it may concern' when the reader is known. An addressed letter is harder to have been written for someone else, and reviewers treat it accordingly.
Signing it yourself as the employee. It becomes a statement about you rather than a verification of you, which is a different document with much less weight.
Sending it from a personal email address. A letter about employment that arrives from a personal account invites the exact verification call the letter was meant to avoid.
Stating a reason for separation. Most employers have a policy against it, it is almost never asked for, and it can only cost the employee.

faq.question: What should an employment verification letter template include?
faq.answer: At minimum: the employee's full legal name, the employer's legal name, the job title and position type, the hire date, the current status, and an authorized signer with a direct phone number. Compensation, hours, and duties are added only where the specific reader has asked for them.

faq.question: Who should write an employment verification letter?
faq.answer: HR, payroll, or a manager with authority to verify on the employer's behalf. An employee can draft it and send it to HR to correct and sign, which usually speeds things up, but the signature has to come from the employer.

faq.question: Should salary be in the letter?
faq.answer: Only when the reader asked for it and the employer is authorized to disclose it. A landlord and a lender normally need it; a new employer's background check normally does not; and a letter that volunteers it to a reader who did not ask has overshared.

faq.question: Do I need a different template for a landlord and a lender?
faq.answer: Yes, in practice. A leasing office wants gross monthly income and a current-status line. An underwriter wants base pay separated from variable pay and will usually also require a verification form, and a letter that blurs the two invites a follow-up condition.

faq.question: What does a self-employed person send instead?
faq.answer: There is no employer to sign, so the equivalent is a paying client confirming the engagement, sent alongside 1099s, the bank record of the deposits, and where the reader will accept one, a CPA letter. Any single one of those on its own settles very little.

faq.question: How long should the letter be?
faq.answer: One page and usually four to six sentences. A verification letter that runs long reads as though it is arguing a case, and a reviewer who reads an argument starts looking for what is being argued around.

pages.title: Proof of Employment Letter
pages.anchorText: Proof of employment: what actually counts
pages.description: A proof of employment letter is the weakest item in the employment evidence stack and the easiest one to obtain. This page ranks the eight things reviewers accept as proof, shows where the letter sits among them, and gives you what to attach so the letter holds.

pages.definition: A proof of employment letter is a signed statement offered as evidence that a person is or was employed. Reviewers rank it below payroll records and tax documents, because it is the only item in the evidence stack that someone types by hand rather than a system producing it.

mistakes: Sending the letter alone. It is the item in the stack a reviewer trusts least, and on its own it produces a verification call and a delay rather than a decision.
Retyping or reformatting a pay stub to make it clearer. A stub that does not look like the payroll system produced it is treated as altered, and the year-to-date arithmetic is checked.
Using the trading name instead of the employer's legal name. When the letter says one name and the W-2 says another, a reviewer has to resolve it, and resolving it takes days.
Offering an offer letter as proof of current employment. It shows a job was offered, not that it started or that it continues.
Staying silent about a document you cannot produce. A reviewer who finds a gap themselves treats it as a gap; a reviewer told about it in advance treats it as a fact of the case.

faq.question: What counts as proof of employment?
faq.answer: Ranked by how reviewers weigh it: an IRS wage and income transcript, pay stubs from the last 30 days, a verification form returned directly by the employer, W-2 forms, an employment verification letter, an offer letter, bank statements showing direct deposit, and last of all a statement you wrote about yourself, which is not evidence.

faq.question: Is a proof of employment letter enough on its own?
faq.answer: Rarely. It is accepted, and then verified by telephone, which costs days. Sent alongside a recent pay stub whose year-to-date figure reconciles with it, the same letter usually closes the question without a call.

faq.question: How do I prove employment for a job I started this year?
faq.answer: The tax record does not exist yet, so the offer letter, the first pay stubs, and a current-status letter have to carry it together. Say plainly in the cover note that no W-2 exists for this employer yet and when the first one will be issued.

faq.question: What if my employer will not give me a letter?
faq.answer: Send the payroll and tax record instead: recent pay stubs, W-2 forms, an IRS wage and income transcript, and bank statements showing the matching deposits. If verification is outsourced, give the reviewer the service name and employer code so they can verify through the route your employer actually uses.

faq.question: Can I write my own proof of employment letter?
faq.answer: You can write it and ask your employer to correct and sign it. What you cannot do is sign it yourself and offer it as proof — a statement you wrote about your own employment is the claim being checked, not evidence for it.

faq.question: Is an automated verification service report the same as a letter?
faq.answer: No, and it is often stronger, because it comes from payroll data rather than from someone typing. It is also a consumer report in this context, so if it is used against your application the Fair Credit Reporting Act gives you the right to be told and to see it.

pages.summary: A letter of explanation is five sentences: what happened, when, why, what it means now, and what is attached. Everything longer than that is either a second condition that needs its own letter or an argument the reviewer did not ask for.
pages.definition: A letter of explanation is a short signed statement answering one specific question a reviewer has raised about your file, structured as five parts: the condition being answered, what happened and when, why it happened, what the current position is, and the documents attached that support all of it.
pages.definitionDetail: The structure matters more than the wording, because a reviewer is not reading for persuasion. They have a condition to clear, and they are looking for the four facts that let them clear it. A letter that buries those facts in a paragraph of context takes three readings; a letter that puts them in order takes one.

keyFacts: One letter answers one condition. If the reviewer raised three, send three letters — a single letter covering all three gets cleared on none of them until the reviewer has separated them for you.
Quote the condition back in the first line, in the reviewer's own words. That is what lets a processor match your letter to the open item without reading the rest of it.
The letter is corroboration, not evidence. It is the attachments that clear the condition; the letter tells the reviewer what the attachments show and in what order to read them.
Never explain something that has not been asked about. Volunteering a second issue opens a second condition, and reviewers are required to document what they learn.
Sign and date it. An unsigned letter of explanation is treated as a draft in most underwriting and benefits workflows, and gets returned rather than read.

steps: Copy the condition into a blank document first. The letter is built around it, and paraphrasing the condition is the fastest way to answer a question nobody asked.

Assemble the five parts in order and stop. Do not add background, apology, or anything about how the application matters to you.
Read it once for anything that could open a new question. Delete that sentence.
Sign it, date it, list the attachments by name and date, and send it by the route the reviewer specified.

faq.question: What should a letter of explanation template include?
faq.answer: Five parts, in order: the condition quoted in the reviewer's own words, what happened and when, why it happened, where the matter stands today, and the documents attached in support. Plus your legal name, the file number, a signature, and a date.

faq.question: How long should a letter of explanation be?
faq.answer: Five to seven sentences for most conditions, and three or four for a narrow one. If it runs past a page, that is usually a sign it is answering more than one condition and should be split.

faq.question: Can one letter cover more than one condition?
faq.answer: It can, but it should not. Conditions are cleared one at a time in the reviewer's system, so a combined letter stays open on all of them until someone separates it. Three conditions means three signed letters and one covering email.

faq.question: Does a letter of explanation need to be signed?
faq.answer: Yes. Most underwriting and benefits workflows treat an unsigned letter as a draft and return it rather than reading it. Sign it, date it, and use the legal name that appears on the application.

faq.question: What if I cannot document part of the explanation?
faq.answer: Say so in the letter, name what does not exist, and offer whatever stands in its place. A reviewer told about a gap in advance treats it as a fact of the case; a reviewer who finds it treats it as a gap.

faq.question: Do I have to use a template at all?
faq.answer: No, but the structure is doing the work. The reviewer is not reading for persuasion — they have one condition to clear and four facts to find. A letter that puts those four facts in a predictable order gets read once.

pages.summary: Answer the condition the underwriter wrote, not the topic it belongs to. A letter about your finances in general, sent against a condition about one deposit on one date, does not clear that condition and usually creates a second one.
pages.definition: A mortgage letter of explanation is a signed statement an underwriter requires when the file contains something the documents alone do not settle — a deposit with no visible source, a gap in employment, a recent credit inquiry, an address that does not reconcile — and the loan cannot be cleared to close until it is answered.
pages.definitionDetail: It is issued as a condition, which means it has a place in a checklist and a person whose job is to close it. That is why the mechanics matter as much as the content: a letter that a processor cannot match to the open condition does not clear it, however well written it is.

A large deposit condition is about the source of the funds, not the amount. Underwriters need to see the money leave an identifiable place and arrive, which usually means a statement from both sides.

Sort the conditions into one letter each, and note which documents each will need before writing anything.

For any funds condition, obtain the record from both sides of the transfer. A statement showing money arriving, with nothing showing it leaving somewhere identifiable, does not close a source-of-funds question.
Write each letter to its condition, quoting the wording, and stop at the point the condition is answered.
Reconcile every figure against the attached statements before you send. A rounded number in the letter against an exact one on the statement causes a second request.
Send them together with one covering email that lists the condition identifiers, and ask the processor to confirm which ones are cleared.
reviewChecklist: Each letter names one condition identifier and answers only that condition.
Every amount in the letter matches the statement to the cent.
A funds explanation shows both sides of the transfer, not only the arrival.
A credit inquiry explanation states directly whether new debt resulted.
Nothing in any letter refers to a matter the underwriter did not raise.

mistakes: Sending one letter for four conditions. Each has an identifier and clears separately, so a combined letter leaves all four open until a processor separates them.
Answering a source-of-funds condition with only the receiving statement. It shows the money arrived; the underwriter is asking where it came from and whether it is borrowed.
Rounding an amount. A letter saying $8,400 against a statement showing $8,412.63 produces a second request rather than a cleared condition.
Using a letter of explanation where a gift letter is required. They are different documents with different required elements, and the substitution is caught every time.
Explaining an issue the underwriter did not raise. It becomes a documented condition on the file, which is the opposite of what volunteering it was meant to achieve.

faq.question: Why does a mortgage underwriter want a letter of explanation?
faq.answer: Because the file contains something the documents alone do not settle — a deposit with no visible source, an employment gap, a recent credit inquiry, an address that does not reconcile. It is issued as a condition, which means the loan cannot be cleared to close until it is answered.

faq.question: What are the most common mortgage letter of explanation requests?
faq.answer: Eight cover almost all of them: a large deposit, credit inquiries within the last 120 days, late payments, an employment gap, an address history discrepancy, a name variation, NSF or overdraft activity, and gift funds.

faq.question: How do I explain a large deposit to an underwriter?
faq.answer: Show both sides of the transfer. Name the sender and your relationship to them, attach the statement from the sending account and the receiving statement, and state directly that the funds are not borrowed and no repayment is owed.

faq.question: Do I need one letter or several?
faq.answer: One per condition. Conditions are tracked and cleared individually, so a single letter covering several of them stays open on all of them until someone unpicks it. Send them together with one covering email listing the identifiers.

faq.question: Is a letter of explanation the same as a gift letter?
faq.answer: No. A gift letter has specific required elements — the donor, the relationship, the amount, and an express statement that no repayment is expected — and lenders will not accept a general explanation in its place.

faq.question: Will a letter of explanation get my mortgage approved?
faq.answer: No. It clears one condition. The credit decision rests on income, assets, the debt-to-income calculation, the appraisal, and the lender's own overlays, none of which any letter can change.

atoms.title: short answer
atoms.text: A mortgage letter of explanation is a signed statement an underwriter requires when the file contains something the documents alone do not settle. It is issued as a condition with its own identifier, and the loan cannot be cleared to close until that condition is answered.

atoms.title: the eight conditions
atoms.text: Eight conditions generate almost every mortgage letter of explanation: a large deposit, credit inquiries within the last 120 days, late payments, an employment gap, an address history discrepancy, a name variation, NSF or overdraft activity, and gift funds. Each needs a different set of facts and different attachments.

atoms.title: source of funds
atoms.text: A large-deposit condition asks where the money came from, not how much it was. What clears it is the statement from the sending account together with the receiving statement and the sender's own confirmation. The receiving statement alone shows arrival, not source, and does not close the question.

atoms.title: mistakes
atoms.text: Letters come back from underwriting for five reasons: one letter was sent for several separately-tracked conditions, a funds explanation showed only the receiving side, an amount was rounded rather than matched to the statement, a letter of explanation was used where a gift letter is required, or an issue nobody raised was volunteered and became a new condition.
